M05.01.title: Pharyngeal regions
M05.01.text: The pharynx has named regions: the nasopharynx behind the nasal cavity, the oropharynx behind the oral cavity, and the laryngopharynx farther down.

M05.01.title: Pharynx terminology
M05.01.text: These regions are not simply alternate names for the nose and mouth.

M05.01.title: Airway and digestive pathway
M05.01.text: The airway shares part of its route with the digestive pathway before the routes separate.

M05.02.title: Larynx and vocal folds
M05.02.text: The larynx contains the vocal folds and connects the pharynx to the trachea.

M05.02.title: Swallowing and epiglottis
M05.02.text: During swallowing, coordinated movements protect the airway; the epiglottis helps cover the laryngeal opening.

M05.05.title: Visceral pleura
M05.05.text: The visceral pleura covers the lung surface.

M05.05.qualification: Supplemental explanation; no corresponding numerical/3D process or clinical prediction.

M05.05.title: Parietal pleura
M05.05.text: The parietal pleura lines the inside of the thoracic wall.

M05.05.qualification: Supplemental explanation; no corresponding numerical/3D process or clinical prediction.

M05.05.title: Pleural fluid and coupling
M05.05.text: A thin fluid layer between them reduces friction and helps the lungs follow movements of the chest wall.

M05.05.qualification: Supplemental explanation; no corresponding numerical/3D process or clinical prediction.

M05.05.title: Pleural potential space
M05.05.text: This is normally a potential space, not a large air-filled gap.

M05.05.qualification: Supplemental explanation; no corresponding numerical/3D process or clinical prediction.

M05.05.title: Air or fluid in pleural space
M05.05.text: Air or excess fluid entering the pleural space can interfere with expansion.

This is the registered four-chamber HRA heart with illustrative continuous residual blood plus the existing closed circulation map. Named itinerary stops teach a journey spanning many beats, not a tracked molecule completing a full circuit in one heartbeat. Lung/systemic exchange insets are separate labeled instructional schematics, not gross source anatomy or a measured gas-transport solver. Blood occupancy is qualitative geometry; pressure/flow/volume come from the shared circulation model.

M05.09.title: Cellular respiration
M05.09.text: Cellular respiration is the chemical process by which cells use energy substrates, often consuming oxygen and producing carbon dioxide.
M05.09.source: Owner-approved adapted M05.09 narration · source script lines 148-175;378-387 · course PDF physical pp75,77,83–84
M05.09.qualification: Supplemental explanation; no corresponding numerical/3D process or clinical prediction.

M05.09.title: Ventilation, exchange and metabolism
M05.09.text: These ideas connect, but they are not interchangeable names for the same event.

M05.09.qualification: Supplemental explanation; no corresponding numerical/3D process or clinical prediction.

M05.10.title: Carbon dioxide and bicarbonate
M05.10.text: Carbon dioxide participates in the bicarbonate buffer system.
M05.10.source: Owner-approved adapted M05.10 narration · source script lines 102-115;148-175 · course PDF physical pp53
M05.10.qualification: Supplemental explanation; no corresponding numerical/3D process or clinical prediction.

M05.10.title: Carbon dioxide retention and pH
M05.10.text: If other factors remain similar, retaining more carbon dioxide tends to lower blood pH, while removing more tends to raise it.
M05.10.source: Owner-approved adapted M05.10 narration · source script lines 102-115;148-175 · course PDF physical pp53
M05.10.qualification: Supplemental explanation; no corresponding numerical/3D process or clinical prediction.

M05.10.title: Arterial pH range
M05.10.text: Arterial blood pH is normally tightly regulated around seven point three five to seven point four five.
M05.10.source: Owner-approved adapted M05.10 narration · source script lines 102-115;148-175 · course PDF physical pp53
M05.10.qualification: Supplemental explanation; no corresponding numerical/3D process or clinical prediction.

M05.10.title: Lungs and kidneys in acid-base regulation
M05.10.text: The lungs and kidneys both contribute to acid-base regulation.

M05.10.qualification: Supplemental explanation; no corresponding numerical/3D process or clinical prediction.

M05.10.text: A visible chest rise alone does not tell us whether ventilation is removing carbon dioxide adequately.
